title: Complete SEO Glossary for 2026: All Key Terms Explained
summary: This complete SEO glossary for September 2026 covers on-page, technical, and AEO terms so your strategy is built on the right vocabulary.
body_markdown:
A lot of SEO confusion comes down to vocabulary, not strategy. When you're not sure what a canonical tag does or why passage-level structure matters, the tactics feel random. Work through the terms first, and the decisions behind them start making a lot more sense.


Stop treating SEO jargon as something you'll just pick up over time. The terms matter because the tactics behind them do, and misreading one (like confusing search intent or skipping schema markup) can quietly tank work you've spent months building. Get the vocabulary right first, and the strategy gets a lot easier to follow.


**TLDR:**


- SEO ranking runs in sequence: crawling, indexing, then ranking. Break one step and the whole chain stops.
- Schema markup is the most overlooked technical fix. Pages without it get filtered by AI engines before content quality is even considered.
- 59.7% of Google searches ended without a click (Similarweb, 2024). Ranking alone doesn't get you traffic anymore.
- Passage-level optimization, self-contained blocks of 130-170 words, determines whether AI engines cite your page or skip it entirely.
- Maintouch tracks citation share across ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and Claude, with a free tier covering 35 prompts across all five engines for one year.


## What Is SEO and Why Does It Matter


SEO stands for search engine optimization: the practice of making your website more visible in search results so people can find you when they're looking for what you offer.


The goal is simple. When someone searches a relevant term, you want your page showing up, not your competitor's. Every tactic in this glossary — from keyword research to schema markup — traces back to that one goal; read our[AEO vs SEO guide](https://maintouch.com/blogs/aeo-vs-seo-guide) to see how those pieces fit.


Search engines like Google rank pages based on hundreds of signals. Some are on your site (content quality, page speed, metadata). Some are off it (who links to you, how authoritative those sources are). SEO is the work of getting both sides right.


It compounds over time. A well-optimized page published today can drive traffic for years with minimal upkeep, unlike paid ads, which stop the moment your budget does.


## Search Engine Basics: Core Terms to Know First


Before anything else clicks, you need to understand what happens when someone types a query and hits enter.


- Crawling: Googlebot follows links across the web, finding pages and reading their content.
- Indexing: Google stores those pages in a massive database. If you're not indexed, you don't exist in search.
- Ranking: When a query fires, Google pulls from the index and orders results by relevance and authority.
- SERP: Search Engine Results Page, the actual page you see after searching.
- Algorithm: The system Google uses to decide that ordering, drawing on hundreds of signals at once.


Crawling comes first. If Google can't crawl your page, it won't index it, and ranking is impossible. The whole chain breaks at step one.


## On-Page SEO Terms


On-page SEO is where most practitioners spend the majority of their time. These are the terms you'll hit constantly inside a CMS or page editor.


- Title tag: The clickable headline shown in search results. Google treats it as a primary relevance signal, so your target keyword belongs here.
- Meta description: The short summary under your title in the SERP. It doesn't directly affect rankings, but it influences click-through rate.
- H1 tag: The main heading on the page itself. One per page, and it should clearly match your topic.
- Anchor text: The clickable words in a hyperlink. Descriptive anchor text tells Google what the destination page is about.
- Canonical tag: A line of code telling Google which version of a page is the "official" one, useful when duplicate content exists across multiple URLs.
- Internal linking: Links between pages on your own site. They distribute authority and help Google understand your site structure.
- Search intent: The reason behind a query, whether informational, navigational, commercial, or transactional. Matching intent is what separates a ranking page from one that gets ignored.
- Above the fold: Content visible without scrolling. It matters for engagement signals Google tracks.


Get these right on every page before worrying about anything more complex.


## Technical SEO Terms


Technical SEO is the layer non-engineers find most intimidating. These terms come up in audits constantly.


- Robots.txt: A file telling crawlers which pages to skip. Block the wrong pages and you'll accidentally hide your best content. Running[technical SEO on autopilot](https://maintouch.com/platform/technical-seo) catches these issues before they compound.
- Sitemap: A list of your URLs submitted to Google so it knows what exists on your site.
- Crawl budget: How many pages Google will crawl in a given period. Large sites with thin or duplicate pages waste it fast.
- Core Web Vitals: Google's page experience metrics covering load speed (LCP), interactivity (INP), and visual stability (CLS).
- Schema markup: Structured data added to your HTML that tells search engines what your content means, beyond what it literally says.
- 301 redirect: A permanent redirect from one URL to another, passing most of the original page's authority along.
- Noindex: A tag instructing Google not to include a page in search results.
- JavaScript SEO: Making sure Google can render and index content that loads via JavaScript, which crawlers handle differently than static HTML.


[Schema markup](https://maintouch.com/blogs/schema-markup-ai-citations) deserves extra attention. Without it, AI search engines deprioritize your pages before content quality is even considered.


## Keyword Research Terms


Keyword research is where SEO strategy either sharpens or falls apart. These are the terms you need to know.


- Search volume: How many times a keyword gets searched per month. High volume sounds attractive until you see the competition you're up against. Choosing the right[keyword research tools](https://maintouch.com/blogs/best-keyword-research-tools) shapes how accurately you read that competition.
- Keyword difficulty: A score estimating how hard it is to rank for a term, based on the authority of pages already ranking for it.
- Long-tail keywords: Longer, more specific phrases with lower search volume but higher intent. Easier to rank for and more likely to convert.
- Keyword cannibalization: When multiple pages on your site compete for the same keyword, splitting authority and leaving Google unsure which page to rank.
- Search intent: The purpose behind a query. A page targeting "best CRM software" needs to be a comparison, not a product page.[Mapping keywords to the buyer journey](https://maintouch.com/blogs/map-keywords-buyer-journey-seo-funnel) clarifies which intent each page should serve.
- SERP features: Anything beyond the standard blue links, including featured snippets, People Also Ask boxes, image packs, and local map results.
- Featured snippet: The answer box at the top of some SERPs. Ranking here means appearing above position one.
- Zero-click search: A query answered directly on the SERP, so the user never visits a site. 59.7% of Google searches ended without a click (Similarweb, 2024).
- Zero-volume queries (ZVQs): Keywords showing no measurable volume in tools like Semrush or Ahrefs, but appearing in Search Console with one or two impressions. A hundred of them, each matching what a buyer asked ChatGPT last week, is a citation strategy.


## Link Building and Authority Terms


Off-page SEO has its own vocabulary, and these terms show up in every audit and link-building conversation.


- Backlink: A link from another site to yours. The more authoritative the source, the more it moves rankings.
- Domain authority: A third-party score (Moz, Ahrefs, and Semrush each have their own version) estimating how well a domain ranks overall. Not a Google metric, but a useful proxy.
- PageRank: Google's original algorithm for scoring page-level authority based on link volume and quality.
- Link juice: Informal term for the authority passed through a link. Dofollow links pass it; nofollow links don't.
- Dofollow vs. nofollow: Dofollow links pass authority. Nofollow links include a tag telling Google not to count the link as a vote.
- Toxic links: Low-quality or spammy backlinks that can drag your rankings down.
- Disavow: A file you submit to Google asking it to ignore specific backlinks pointing to your site.
- Inbound vs. outbound links: Inbound links come from other sites to yours. Outbound links go from your site to others.


Without[high quality backlinks](https://maintouch.com/blogs/high-quality-backlinks-types-and-tips) from credible sources, even well-structured content rarely surfaces.


## Content SEO Terms


Content strategy has its own term set, and E-E-A-T sits at the top.


- E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trust): The framework Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines use to assess content quality, especially for health, finance, and safety topics. First-hand experience is the newest addition and the hardest to fake.
- Topical authority: How deeply your site covers a subject area. A site with 40 articles on one topic outranks a site with one article on the same topic, all else equal.
- Thin content: Pages with little substance relative to what a searcher needs. Google actively demotes them.
- Duplicate content: Identical or near-identical content on multiple URLs, confusing Google about which version to rank.
- Fresh content: Recency matters for time-sensitive topics. Pages updated in the last 90 days get cited in AI results far more often than stale ones.
- Helpful content: Google's term for content written for people, not search engines. Its Helpful Content system targets sites that produce content primarily to rank instead of genuinely answer questions.


E-E-A-T isn't a score you can check. It's a signal pattern Google infers from author credentials, original research, site reputation, and factual accuracy across your whole domain.


## SEO Metrics and Measurement Terms


Reporting on SEO without knowing these terms means you're reading a map in the wrong language.


- Organic traffic: Visitors arriving from unpaid search results.
- Impressions: How many times your page appeared in a SERP, whether clicked or not. Tracking[AI visibility metrics and KPIs](https://maintouch.com/blogs/ai-visibility-kpis-track-results) alongside these adds the layer most dashboards miss.
- Click-through rate (CTR): Clicks divided by impressions. A high-impression, low-CTR page usually has a weak title tag or mismatched intent.
- Keyword ranking: Your page's position in search results for a specific query.
- SERP position: The numbered slot your page holds. Position one gets the most clicks; below ten gets almost none.
- Dwell time: How long a visitor stays before returning to the SERP. Longer dwell time signals relevance.
- Bounce rate: The share of sessions where a visitor left without interacting further. Context matters; a blog post read in full and then closed isn't a problem.
- Google Search Console (GSC): Google's free tool showing impressions, clicks, CTR, and average position for every query your site ranks for. It's the closest thing to ground truth you have.
- GA4: Google's analytics tool tracking what visitors do after they land: sessions, engagement rate, conversions.


GSC tells you how you're showing up. GA4 tells you what happens after. You need both.


## Local SEO Terms


Local SEO runs on different rules than standard web search. Proximity, relevance, and business data accuracy drive rankings here; backlinks and content are only part of the picture.


- Google Business Profile (GBP): Your free listing in Google's local search system. Name, location, hours, photos, and reviews all live here. It's the single most important local ranking factor.
- Local pack: The map and three-listing block Google shows for location-based queries like "coffee shop near me." Appearing here is separate from ranking in organic results below it.
- NAP consistency: Name, Location, Phone number. These must match exactly across every directory, citation, and mention online. Inconsistencies confuse Google about which location data to trust.
- Citations: Mentions of your business across directories like Yelp, TripAdvisor, and industry-specific listings. Unlike link building, citations don't require a backlink to carry weight.
- Local landing pages: Dedicated pages built for specific cities or regions, targeting location-modified keywords like "accountant in Austin."


NAP consistency is the one most businesses get wrong quietly. The listing looks fine, but a stale location entry on a minor directory is enough to dilute trust.


## Algorithm Updates and Penalties: Key Terms


Google's algorithm isn't one system. It's a stack of overlapping signals, and several named updates target specific abuse patterns.


- Panda targets thin, duplicate, and low-quality content. Sites with large amounts of weak pages get hit across the whole domain.
- Penguin targets manipulative link profiles. Spammy or bought links that violate Google's guidelines can trigger ranking drops sitewide.
- Helpful Content Update targets content written to rank and not genuinely help readers. Sites with high volumes of AI-generated filler content are particularly exposed.
- Core updates are broad algorithm changes Google releases periodically with no single target. Rankings can shift sharply, and the fix is usually content quality, not a technical tweak.
- Manual penalties happen when a human reviewer at Google flags your site for a specific violation. Unlike algorithmic demotions, these come with a notification in GSC and require a reconsideration request to resolve.


The white hat vs. black hat distinction cuts through most of this quickly. White hat SEO follows Google's guidelines: earning links, writing for readers, building real authority over time. Black hat SEO exploits loopholes, and it tends to work until it doesn't.


Common black hat tactics worth knowing by name:


- Keyword stuffing: Cramming a keyword into a page unnaturally to rank for it. Google catches this easily.
- Cloaking: Showing different content to search engines than to users. An automatic manual penalty if caught.
- Link schemes: Buying, trading, or manufacturing backlinks at scale to fake authority.
- PBNs (Private Blog Networks): Networks of sites built solely to manufacture backlinks. High risk, diminishing returns.


The pattern across all penalties is the same: Google's guidelines reward sites that behave as if the algorithm doesn't exist.


## AI Search and AEO Terms for 2026


59.7% of Google searches ended without a click (Similarweb, 2024). Most glossaries haven't caught up to what that shift actually requires. Here are the terms you need to know.


- [Answer Engine Optimization](https://maintouch.com/blogs/what-is-answer-engine-optimization-complete-guide) (AEO): Optimizing content to get cited inside AI-generated answers, instead of only ranking in blue links.
- AI Overviews: Google's AI-generated summaries appearing above organic results, pulling from multiple sources simultaneously.
- Citation share: How often your brand appears in AI-generated answers versus competitors. The AEO equivalent of ranking position.
- Passage-level optimization: Structuring content in self-contained blocks of roughly 130-170 words so AI engines can extract and cite a single chunk without surrounding context.
- Query fan-out: How AI engines break one prompt into multiple sub-queries, run them in parallel, and assemble an answer from the best-matching passages.
- Schema for AI: Structured data (FAQPage, HowTo, Article) that signals to AI retrieval systems which content to pull. Pages without it get filtered out before content quality is even considered.
- Zero-click search: Queries answered on the SERP itself, with no site visit required.
- AI citations: When a chatbot or AI Overview references your page as a source in its generated answer.

You can hold a first-page ranking and still be absent from AI answers if your content structure doesn't support passage-level extraction.


## SEO Tools and Platforms: Common Terms


- SEO audit: A systematic review of your site's technical health, on-page optimization, and backlink profile. Most tools surface the issues; fewer actually fix them. Comparing the[best AEO tools](https://maintouch.com/blogs/best-aeo-tools) helps identify which close that gap.
- Crawl report: Output from a crawler like Screaming Frog or Ahrefs showing broken links, redirect chains, missing metadata, and indexability problems across every URL.
- Keyword gap analysis: Comparing your keyword rankings against competitors to find terms they rank for that you don't. This is typically the input to a content roadmap.
- Rank tracker: A tool monitoring your SERP positions over time for a set of target keywords. Useful for spotting ranking movement after publishing or updating content.
- Backlink checker: A tool showing which sites link to you or a competitor, with metrics like domain authority and anchor text distribution.
- Site authority metrics: Domain Authority (Moz), Domain Rating (Ahrefs), and Authority Score (Semrush) are third-party estimates of ranking potential based on backlink profiles. None are Google metrics.
- Search Console integration: Connecting GSC to a third-party tool to pull impression, click, and ranking data directly. Without it, keyword difficulty and volume estimates stay directional, never accurate.
- Programmatic SEO: Automatically generating hundreds or thousands of optimized pages from templates and structured data, targeting geo-specific or long-tail query clusters at scale.


The distinction worth keeping in mind across all of these: most tools surface data and stop. A rank tracker shows you slipping. A crawl report flags the broken redirect. Closing the loop by actually fixing the redirect or updating the page is a separate workflow unless the tool you're using executes it directly.

## FAQ


### How does AEO differ from traditional SEO in terms of what content actually gets cited?


Traditional SEO ranks pages by relevance and authority signals like backlinks and keyword placement. AEO determines which specific passages get pulled into AI-generated answers, and the selection criteria are different: AI engines look for self-contained chunks of 130-170 words that answer one question completely, schema markup like FAQPage and HowTo, and structured formats like comparison tables and checklists. A page can hold a first-page Google ranking and still be absent from AI answers if it lacks passage-level structure and clean structured data.


### What's the best SEO automation tool for a seed-stage startup that can't afford a full-time SEO hire?


If budget is the constraint, the straightforward answer is to start with Google Search Console (free) and a crawl tool to get your technical baseline, then layer in content execution. The mistake most early-stage teams make is buying a reporting tool when what they actually need is execution: a rank tracker tells you you're slipping, but someone or something still has to fix the page. Maintouch replaces the full labor stack (writer, editor, technical SEO, link building) at a fraction of full-time headcount cost, which is why it's built for founder-led and venture-backed companies that want a running SEO program without hiring a team to run it.


### Should I update old blog posts or write new content when existing posts get no organic traffic?


Start with the posts sitting in positions 11-20 in Google Search Console, where you're already indexed but not clicking. Those pages need tightening, not replacement: update the metadata, sharpen the opening to match search intent directly, add internal links from higher-authority pages, and refresh any stale facts or stats. Brand-new content makes sense when there's no existing coverage of a topic; updating makes sense when Google already knows the page exists but hasn't decided it's good enough. Stale pages (90-plus days without an update) also get cited far less often in AI-generated answers, so freshness is a two-channel problem.


### How do zero-volume queries (ZVQs) work, and why do they matter for AI citation strategy?


Zero-volume queries are keywords that show no measurable search volume in Semrush or Ahrefs but appear in Search Console with one or two impressions. Those impressions signal that a real person typed that exact phrase, which is often what a buyer asked ChatGPT or Perplexity before running a Google search. A hundred ZVQs, each matching an actual buyer question, is a map of exactly what AI engines are fielding in your category. Content built around them answers the questions AI tools are already being asked, which is the direct causal input for getting cited instead of a competitor.


### What does a complete SEO solution include beyond content creation?


Content is one layer. A complete SEO program also covers technical health (metadata, canonical tags, schema, redirects, page speed), backlink acquisition from credible sources, AI citation tracking across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude, and ongoing content refresh as pages age or facts change. Most tools handle one or two of these and hand the rest back to you. The practical test is simple: after the tool delivers its output, does the loop close automatically, or does someone have to pick up the work and route it to a developer, an agency, or a spreadsheet?


### Which schema types should I add first on a large site?


Start with schema that directly influences answer engines: FAQPage, HowTo, Article, and Product where relevant. Prioritize pages with high impressions in Google Search Console and roll schema via templates so the work scales without manual edits.


### How often should I refresh pages to keep AI citations coming?


For time-sensitive topics, refresh within about 90 days; for evergreen pages, review every 6–12 months or after any material product or fact change. Freshness is a clear signal in AI overviews and helps pages stay eligible for citation.


### What's the easiest way to structure passages so AI engines will cite them?


Write self-contained 130–170 word blocks that answer one question directly, lead with the answer sentence, and sit under a clear H3 heading. Add FAQPage/HowTo schema or a short checklist to make extraction easier for retrieval systems.


### Does adding schema guarantee I'll be cited by AI engines?


No. Schema is often required but not sufficient — you also need extractable passage structure, factual accuracy, and enough topical authority. Treat schema as a gating signal that lets engines consider your content, not as the thing that wins citation by itself.


### How do I find zero-volume queries that are actually useful?


Use Google Search Console: filter queries with very low impressions and look for conversational phrasing or exact questions. Those ZVQs often match what people ask chatbots and make a practical map for passages you want cited.


### Should I focus on ranking or citation share first?


Do both, but prioritize making target pages citable first: passage structure and schema. You can rank without being cited, but you can't be cited if your passages aren't extractable — fix the structure, then shore up backlinks and on-page relevance.


### Can AI engines cite content that loads via JavaScript?


They can, but only if the rendered HTML contains the passage and schema Google can index. Use server-side rendering or reliable prerendering, then verify in Search Console that the final HTML includes the content and structured data you expect.


### How should I measure whether my citation share is improving?


Track citations and mentions in AI Overviews and chat outputs across engines, and watch GSC for rising impressions on related ZVQs and passage queries. Tools that aggregate engine citations (the post mentions Maintouch as one example) speed this work, but start with a manual baseline if you don't yet have a monitoring tool.
